What conceptual and methodological pitfalls arise when computational text analysis is used to study social and cultural questions, and how can they be avoided?

A cross-disciplinary reflection, by computer and social scientists, on how to analyze text as social and cultural data - covering question framing, measurement validity, annotation, and interpretation - bridging NLP with the humanities and social sciences.

quote: In this article we have consolidated our experiences, as scholars from very different disciplines, in analyzing text as social and cultural data and described how the research process often unfolds.
Second, we hope to provide a set of key questions that can guide work with thick social and cultural concepts.

value: Where there is no objective standard, accuracy against annotations measures consistency rather than correctness
quote: Accuracy, as well as other measures such as precision, recall and F-score, are sometimes presented as a measure of validity, but if we do not have a genuinely objective determination of what something is supposed measure—as is often the case in text analysis—then accuracy is perhaps a better indication of reliability than of validity.

value: Inter-annotator reliability differs from accuracy in taking no coder as correct and discounting agreement expected by chance
quote: In contrast, when the reliability is measured based on the output of different annotators, no coder is taken as the standard and the likelihood of coders reaching agreement by chance (rather than because they are “correct”) is factored into the resulting statistic.

value: Validation without a gold standard proceeds by sampling across the full range of scores and asking whether each case makes sense under the adopted definition
quote: That is, take a stratified random sample, selecting observations from the full range of scores, and ask: Do these make sense in light of the systematized concept?

value: Reading the texts beside the model output informs the model as much as the model informs the reading

Reliability aims to capture repeatability, i.e., the extent to which a given tool provides consistent results.
Validity assesses the extent to which a given measurement tool measures what it is supposed to measure.
The collection of annotation choices make up an annotation scheme (or “codebook”).
In line with Adcock and Collier's notion of “content validity” (Adcock and Collier, 2001 ), the goal is to assess whether the codebook adequately captures the systematized concept.
